analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from using credit checks in hiring and firing decisions, with narrow exceptions.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar employers from using credit checks in hiring was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in July 2019, drew 7 cosponsors, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop credit reporting agencies from selling employers credit reports about a worker's or applicant's creditworthiness for use in hiring, firing, or other job decisions. Employers could still use credit reports only in narrow cases — jobs requiring eligibility for classified information or where the law requires it — and only with the worker's authorization. It also says an employer cannot reject someone simply for refusing to authorize a credit check.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants and current employees whose credit has been damaged by job loss, medical bills, divorce, or other life events. Under current law, an employer can buy a credit report and decline to hire someone because of it, even when credit history has nothing to do with the job. The bill would end that practice for nearly all positions, while preserving credit checks for national-security-related jobs and wherever the law requires them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Job seekers and workers with damaged credit

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing employers a credit report bearing on a person's creditworthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity when the employer intends to use it for an employment decision.

Keeps a narrow exception: an employer may still use a credit report, with the worker's authorization, if the job requires eligibility for access to classified information or if the use is otherwise required by law.
Bars an employer from denying someone a job or making any other employment decision against them because they declined to authorize a credit check.

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies and background-screening firms lose the market for employment credit reports, since agencies could no longer sell reports for use in most job decisions. Employers also lose credit history as a screening tool, except for classified-information positions and cases where the law requires a check.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and employers using credit screens

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose credit history as a screening signal for nearly all jobs. The only exceptions in the bill are positions requiring eligibility for classified information and uses otherwise required by law, which is narrower than the exemptions some state laws allow for jobs handling money or sensitive finances.

The bill stops credit reports from being used in hiring but does nothing about the underlying problems — it does not fix errors in credit reports or change what debts, such as medical bills, appear on them — so people with damaged credit still face barriers everywhere else credit is checked, like renting an apartment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gain is concrete: a bad credit history — often the residue of a job loss or medical bills — could no longer be used to deny them nearly any job. The cost falls on a small set of companies that sell employment credit reports and on employers who lose one screening signal; the classified-information exception preserves checks where national security is genuinely at stake. On balance the trade favors workers, and the bill's design is narrow rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Equal Employment for All Act of 2019 in the House on July 19, 2019.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services — the only action the bill ever received.
The committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor; it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies and background-screening firms keep their employment credit report business, and employers keep the ability to screen applicants by credit history.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus keep selling employment credit reports

for.name: 7 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; the action history shows no committee action after the initial referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans, but the bill never got a vote in committee or on the floor, so where each party actually stood was never tested.

industries.note: These agencies sell employment credit reports to employers as a paid product. The bill cuts off that use for nearly all job decisions, eliminating a slice of their revenue. Their interest in keeping the market runs against workers who want credit history left out of hiring.
Screening firms buy credit data from the bureaus and resell it as part of pre-employment background checks. Banning credit-based employment reports removes part of their product line.

industries.industry: Employers that use credit checks in hiring
industries.note: Employers would lose credit history as a screening tool, except for classified-information jobs and where the law requires checks. Some argue it helps them judge reliability; workers experience it as a barrier to jobs based on debts that often came from job loss or medical bills.
